surveyDefinition.title: Meal Kit Delivery Services — consumer survey (North America)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on meal kit usage patterns, purchase and subscription behaviour, and the motivations driving their choice of meal kit service.

segments.name: Convenience-Driven Households
segments.description: Order meal kits primarily to save time and reduce the mental load of meal planning. They value quick preparation, minimal cleanup, and reliable delivery. They are less interested in culinary exploration and more in getting dinner on the table efficiently.

segments.name: Culinary Adventurers
segments.description: Use meal kits to explore new cuisines, learn cooking techniques, and access specialty ingredients. They are motivated by recipe novelty, flavour complexity, and the experience of cooking. They are less price-sensitive and more willing to try premium or seasonal menus.

segments.name: Diet-Focused Users
segments.description: Select meal kits that align with specific dietary needs or health goals, such as keto, vegan, or low-calorie. They are motivated by nutritional control, portion accuracy, and avoiding unwanted ingredients. They are willing to pay a premium for dietary compliance.

segments.name: Budget-Conscious Households
segments.description: Use meal kits as a way to manage household food spending and reduce food waste. They are highly price-sensitive, compare cost per meal against grocery shopping, and are motivated by promotions and family-friendly pricing. They are less loyal and more likely to pause or cancel when budgets tighten.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Meal Kit Delivery Services buyers in North America. It asks how people use Meal Kit Delivery Services, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in North America who buy or use Meal Kit Delivery Services for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Currently subscribed to or have used a meal kit delivery service in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for household food purchases; Aged 18 or older; Responsible for at least some household meal preparation. Excluded: Professional chefs or restaurant owners purchasing for commercial use; Individuals who have never used or considered a meal kit service; Businesses or institutions buying meal kits for employees or events; People under 18.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Household consumers buy meal kits for their own home cooking, pay for them via subscription or one-time purchase, and decide which service to use based on their own preferences. Businesses do not purchase meal kits on behalf of consumers, and there is no meaningful B2B motion in this category.
respondentBehaviours: Value convenience and time savings over grocery shopping and meal planning
Interested in cooking but lack time or inspiration for meal prep
Open to trying new recipes and cuisines
Willing to pay a premium for pre-portioned ingredients and recipe cards
Often health-conscious or have specific dietary preferences (e.g., vegetarian, keto, low-calorie)
May be influenced by promotional offers, discounts, or free trials
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Meal Kit Usage & Household Context
sections.covers: Establishes how respondents use meal kits, for whom, and what role they play in the household's weekly meal routine.

sections.label: Subscription Acquisition & Management
sections.covers: Covers how respondents started, manage, and pay for their meal kit subscriptions, including triggers, channels, and spend.

sections.label: Meal Kit Requirements & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Explores what respondents need from a meal kit service—recipes, customization, packaging, and value—and the trade-offs they are willing to make.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Churn Risk
sections.covers: Measures overall satisfaction, specific pain points, switching triggers, and future subscription intent.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with meal kits and the context in which they are used, then moves through the purchase and subscription journey, explores product and service requirements, and closes with satisfaction and future intent. This arc allows the study to classify respondents into four behavioural segments based on their motivations and usage patterns.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Meal Kit Delivery Services in North America — who Currently subscribed to or have used a meal kit delivery service in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for household food purchases; Aged 18 or older; Responsible for at least some household meal preparation. The audience is defined as household consumers who make their own food purchasing decisions and are the end users of meal kit services. The focus is on current or recent users to capture real experiences and preferences, with demographic filters to ensure relevance to the typical meal kit market.

notes: All four segments have at least two scoring options and at least one 3-point option.
Only options that clearly discriminate were scored; many neutral options were left unscored.
Some options like 'I was tired of the same meals' were not scored because they could apply to both culinary adventurers and convenience seekers.
Budget-conscious planners are identified by price sensitivity, food waste reduction, and promotion-seeking behaviours.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with meal kits and the context in which they are used, then moves through the purchase and subscription journey, explores product and service requirements, and closes with satisfaction and future intent. This arc allows the study to classify respondents into four behavioural segments based on their motivations and usage patterns.
storyline_notes: Added a dedicated beat on subscription management (skip, pause, cancel) because meal kits are a subscription service and this behaviour is central to churn risk.
Included a beat on dietary and sustainability credentials to capture the needs of diet-focused and eco-conscious users, which are key differentiators in this category.
Emphasised delivery frequency and flexibility in the purchase behaviour section, as this is a key operational aspect of meal kits in North America.
The satisfaction section includes a beat on switching triggers specific to meal kits (menu fatigue, price increases, dietary gaps) to support churn prediction.
The segments are designed to be separable by questions on motivations (need_state), decision drivers, trade-offs, and future intent.
metadata.classification_reason: Household consumers buy meal kits for their own home cooking, pay for them via subscription or one-time purchase, and decide which service to use based on their own preferences. Businesses do not purchase meal kits on behalf of consumers, and there is no meaningful B2B motion in this category.
